lead: A thin spherical shell under internal pressure has the same direct stress on every plane through its centre: σ = p d/(4t). This is half the hoop stress of a cylinder with the same d, t and p. Strain is equal in every surface direction, so volume strain is 3ε. Gas holders and dished vessel ends use this.
prereq: You need 7.5 for cylinder stress and strain, and Unit 1 for volumetric strain and Hooke's law.

sections.h3: Cut the shell through its centre

blocks.text: A shell is thin when t ≤ d/20; d is internal diameter and t wall thickness, both in mm. p is internal pressure in N/mm² (MPa). The wall carries only direct tension; bending is ignored.

items: Cut the sphere into halves through its centre.
Pressure on one half is F = p × πd²/4; the curved surface projects to a circle of diameter d.
The cut face is a ring of area πdt, carrying force σ × πdt.
Equate: σdt = pd²/4, so σ = pd/(4t).

blocks.text: Any diametral plane gives the same σ. A sphere has no weak direction. No shear acts on a diametral plane, so σ is a principal stress and the other surface principal stress equals it.

blocks.where: σ is direct stress, N/mm²; p is internal pressure, N/mm²; d is internal diameter, mm; t is wall thickness, mm; r = d/2 is internal radius, mm.

blocks.text: The shell looks the same in every surface direction. The direct stress σ is the same in two perpendicular directions in the surface; radial stress is taken as zero. Hence ε = (σ/E)(1 − ν).

blocks.where: ε is linear strain in any surface direction; σ = pd/(4t) is direct stress, N/mm²; E is Young's modulus, N/mm² (2×10⁵ for steel); ν is Poisson's ratio (about 0.3 for steel).

blocks.text: Every internal diameter grows by ε. A cube argument gives (1+ε)³ ≈ 1+3ε for small ε, so

blocks.where: V = πd³/6 is internal volume; dV is increase. With d in metres V is in m³; with d in mm V is in mm³.

blocks.text: A cylinder is less simple: V = (π/4)d²L, so

blocks.where: ε_h = (σ_h/E)(1 − ν/2); ε_L = (σ_L − ν σ_h)/E; σ_h = pd/(2t); σ_L = pd/(4t); V = (π/4)d²L.

sections.h3: Sphere against cylinder, and dished ends

blocks.text: With the same d, t, p and ν = 0.3, the sphere gives dV/V = 0.525 pd/(tE); the cylinder gives 0.95 pd/(tE). The sphere swells 55% as much and has half the wall stress, so it needs half the plate thickness.

A hemispherical end (or the spherical crown of a dished head) is part of a sphere welded to the cylinder. A flat end would bend and need much thicker plate. The hemispherical end carries tension at pd/(4t), half the shell's hoop stress. The two parts grow differently: shell radial strain ≈ 0.85σ_h/E (σ_h = pd/(2t)), end ≈ 0.35σ_h/E. The stiffer end restrains the shell, so bending and shear appear near the joint. A knuckle radius or thickened transition spreads it.

A sphere has least surface area for a given volume, so it needs least steel per cubic metre stored. It also sits on a small foundation ring. Large LPG and CNG terminals use spheres. Road tankers stay cylindrical because a sphere will not fit on a truck.

figure.caption: Both shells are 2 m diameter and 10 mm thick, with E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.3. At 1.5 MPa the cylinder line reads 1.43 × 10⁻³ and the sphere line only 0.79 × 10⁻³.

spec.aria: Volume strain against internal pressure for a cylinder and a sphere of the same diameter and thickness; the sphere line is flatter, so the sphere swells less.

examples.question: A thin spherical shell of internal diameter 2 m and wall thickness 10 mm holds gas at 1.5 MPa. Take E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.3. Find (i) direct stress, (ii) linear strain, (iii) volume strain, (iv) increase in volume in litres. (v) State the volume strain a thin cylinder of the same d, t and p would show.
steps: Data: p = 1.5 MPa = 1.5×10⁶ N/m², d = 2 m, t = 10 mm = 0.01 m, E = 200 GPa = 2×10¹¹ N/m², ν = 0.3. Thin check: t/d = 0.005, far below 1/20.
examples.answer: σ = 75 MPa, ε = 2.625×10⁻⁴, dV/V = 7.875×10⁻⁴ with ΔV = 3.30 litres; the same-size cylinder would give dV/V = 1.425×10⁻³, about 1.8 times more.
examples.check:
import math
p = 1.5e6
d = 2.0
t = 0.01
E = 200e9
nu = 0.3
sigma = p*d/(4*t)
eps = (sigma/E)*(1-nu)
vol_strain = 3*eps
V = math.pi*d**3/6
dV = vol_strain*V
sh = p*d/(2*t)
eh = (sh/E)*(1-nu/2)
el = (sh/(2*E))*(1-2*nu)
vol_cyl = 2*eh + el
print(round(sigma/1e6, 4))
print(round(eps, 10))
print(round(vol_strain, 10))
print(round(V, 3))
print(round(dV*1000, 2))
print(round(vol_cyl, 10))

traps: Writing σ = pd/(2t) for a sphere. That is a cylinder's hoop stress; a sphere carries pd/(4t).
Using dV/V = ε_h + ε_L for a cylinder. The diameter grows in two directions, so it is 2ε_h + ε_L.
Dropping the Poisson factor: use (σ/E)(1 − ν) for a sphere, (σ_h/E)(1 − ν/2) for a cylinder's hoop direction.
Feeding r into a formula written for d. pd/(4t) = pr/(2t); mixing radius and diameter doubles or halves the answer.
Mixing units: p in MPa (N/mm²) with d in metres. Work in N and mm, or N and m, never half of each.

quiz.q: Write the direct stress in a thin spherical shell of internal diameter d and thickness t under internal pressure p, and define the symbols.
quiz.a: σ = pd/(4t), where σ is wall stress in N/mm², p internal pressure in N/mm², d internal diameter in mm and t wall thickness in mm.

quiz.q: How is the volume strain of a thin sphere related to its linear strain, and what is its internal volume in terms of d?
quiz.a: dV/V = 3ε, and V = πd³/6, so dV = 3ε × πd³/6.

quiz.q: Why is the wall stress in a sphere half that in a cylinder of the same d, t and p?
quiz.a: A cylinder's pressure on projected area dL is held by two wall strips of area tL each, giving resisting area 2t per projected width d. The sphere's pressure on πd²/4 is held by ring area πdt, giving 4t per d, twice as much, hence half the stress.

quiz.q: Why does the volume strain of a thin cylinder contain 2ε_h and not ε_h?
quiz.a: V = (π/4)d²L, so dV/V = 2δd/d + δL/L = 2ε_h + ε_L. The cross-section grows along two perpendicular diameters, so hoop strain enters twice.

quiz.q: A thin spherical shell has d = 1 m, t = 6 mm, p = 1.2 MPa, E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3. Find stress, linear strain, volume strain and increase in volume.
Same data but for a thin cylinder: d = 1 m, t = 6 mm, p = 1.2 MPa. Find its volume strain and compare.
A hemispherical end is welded to a cylindrical shell of the same thickness and material. Membrane stresses at the joint are below allowable, yet cracks start at the weld. Why?
quiz.a: The parts swell differently. The shell grows radially by about 0.85σ_h/E and the end by about 0.35σ_h/E, so the cylinder tries to grow 2.4 times as much. The weld forces them together, producing local bending and shear on each side. Total stress there is membrane plus discontinuity stress. A thicker transition or knuckle radius reduces it.

quiz.q: Large gas stores in terminals are spheres although cylinders are easier to build. Give the reasons.
quiz.a: A sphere has least surface area for a given volume, so plate area per cubic metre stored is least. Its stress is pd/(4t), half a cylinder's, so the same pressure and diameter need half the thickness. Stress is equal in every direction, with no weak seam. The base is a small ring, not a long saddle line. Cylinders win only where space is long and low, or on vehicles.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real design checks discontinuity regions at nozzles, supports and end junctions by finite element analysis of shells of revolution, because the membrane formula assumes a smooth, unperforated shell. Dished ends follow standard profiles — hemispherical, ellipsoidal, torispherical — whose knuckle region is checked separately for bending.
